TOM HOMAN, BORDER CZAR: Now, those are the facts. I don't think he should ever have cleared vetting. You know, when they hire somebody, put them through a vetting process and look at all that stuff. So, I know, based on that information, that that's part of the ongoing investigation.

ICE has about 30,000 employees. They all go through vetting. This is -- this is a -- kind of a rare instance.

HILL: You just heard Tom Homan there calling it a rare instance. Is it an isolated instance or could there be a bigger problem brewing?

Joining the group chat with us now, Marc Caputo, White House reporter with "Axios."

As we look at where things stand, and whether this is an isolated incident. Last night I spoke with Democratic Congressman Shri Thanedar, who serves on House Homeland Security, and he was very clear to me that he does not think this is isolated. Take a listen.

REP. SHRI THANEDAR (D-MI): This is absolutely not an isolated incident. They had a deliberate system that encouraged hiring of people that had, you know, questionable backgrounds.

Background search was not done enough. And ICE agents were hired in a hurry because they wanted to make up that quota that President Trump has set.

HILL: So, we heard his claim here, this is about boosting the numbers to get to a number that President Trump wanted. Did the vetting -- is there evidence that the vetting process writ large has actually suffered in that process?

MARC CAPUTO, WHITE HOUSE REPORTER, "AXIOS": Well, there's evidence that it happened because now there's a person who's dead. But there's a broader issue that ICE and the administration are facing, which is that the American people have increasingly lost confidence, not just in ICE as an agency. I think YouGov recently had 48 percent of Americans thought ICE should be abolished, and only 40 percent said it should be around. But, politically speaking, Republicans have now lost what used to be a sizable advantage on who's best to handle immigration, Republicans or Democrats. According to a Fox poll last week, Democrats now have an inside the error margin of lead of one point on that issue.

So, in addition to that, ICE also is perceived as having, and the immigration system at large, a culture problem. Remember, it's not just Guerrero who got shot. It was also two U.S. citizens who got shot and killed in Minnesota. And before that, there were shootings in Chicago. Is you have immigration agents who are placed in a situation where they wind up doing traffic stops that they're not really trained for, and shootings happen.

HILL: So, to that point, there was the issue of vetting. There's also the issue of training, right?

Sara, you were going to say something?

FISCHER: Well, I was just going to say, on the training point, this has been very well documented that the number of days that it took to get trained as an ICE officer has been reduced dramatically in the Trump era in order to make sure that they have enough agents that can get out to address some of these crises. We've seen a large pullback. But you'll remember, early on in Trump's second term, there was an ICE operation in a different city almost every week. And so, because of that, they needed to get these ICE officers out.

I think the number of days for training went down to 40 something, then it was reduced before, as opposed to many months long training. That completely changes the way that an officer is going to react in any situation.

HILL: And we saw that as a significant focus of questioning, right? I mean I can remember watching some of the hearings over the last however many months, right, that that was a question about. Talk to me about the training. Talk to me about why the training changed. Why the number of days changed. Tom Homan did talk about training practices as well, saying that they're under review. Here's how he put it.

TOM HOMAN, BORDER CZAR: Markwayne Mullin made a decision, well, let's do a temporary pause and make sure, you know, we -- officers have what they need to be safe and do the most safe, secure arrests where possible. And, you know, that review was done pretty quickly. President Trump also said we're going to -- we're going to continue doing vehicle stops because that's a necessary tool in the tool shed. But we always evaluate training.

HILL: You know, you were talking about the training for vehicle stops. The intersect -- "The Intercept," excuse me, obtained internal -- an internal agency wide email from last week about new training for ICE officers, which reads in part, "the officer or officers conducting the stop must have successfully completed an ICE--administered vehicle stop training."

There are a lot of questions about the rhetoric is going out there. Apparently, the directives are out there. But is there actually follow through? Do you see any of what has transpired over the last couple of weeks leading to more thorough reviews here?

DAVISON: That certainly has not played out on the field. You know, we've really seen a ramp up of ICE related violence, versus a cool down after we saw in Minneapolis earlier this year. But this raises a lot of questions. You know, we're starting to see some daylight between ICE and Homan and the White House here. You know, we saw this last week when after, you know, this traffic stop involved shooting that ICE said, look, were going to put a pause on this while we figure out what's going on. Trump came out the next morning and said, nope, we're not going to do that. We're going to continue, you know, everything that ICE was doing before. Again you have -- you know, this is not really an admission of guilt from Homan here about the vetting, but at least suggesting that there could be problems with the process really will be interesting to see how Trump reacts to that. You know, ICE has, in his mind, sort of been infallible here. And you're starting to see the head of ICE, the guy that Trump put in place to run this program, saying, hey, we may have gotten over our skis a little bit.

HILL: It is also fascinating, to Marc's point, Francessca, when we look at, like, Democrats are gaining a little bit when it comes to handling of immigration. You know, Donald Trump has a really good narrative in some areas on immigration in terms of fulfilling campaign promises, right? What we're seeing at the borders. This is not sitting quite so well.

CHAMBERS: This has typically been one of Republicans' best issue areas --

CAPUTO: One hundred percent.

CHAMBERS: As we've seen in the past. I mean this is largely what Donald Trump launched his first campaign on was about immigration. And so certainly heading into the midterms, this is something that, you know, Republicans want to wrestle control back over in terms of a topic for Republican voters.

But with respect to the daylight that you were talking about between, you know, the White House and ICE, I mean, we've seen in the past too where they haven't -- have made announcements and President Trump has said, and the White House has said, nope, that's not how we're going to be handling deportations when it comes to, you know, farm agricultural workers and other things like this.

So, all along we've seen that the White House and the president have typically been setting the policies when it comes to immigration in this country.

HILL: Also want to talk to you about what we are seeing in terms of Democrats.

[06:55:03] Senator Bernie Sanders standing by his coalition of candidates, even as some Democrats worry that the so-called Bernie bros could tank the midterms.

Obamas former chief of staff, Rahm Emanuel, making that argument in a "Wall Street Journal" op-ed over the weekend, blaming the Bernie bros. Adding for the division -- adding, "if the Bernie bros were serious about growing jobs and wages, they would support candidates touting substantive ways to help families." Senator Sanders, firing back.

SEN. BERNIE SANDERS (I-VT): You are an establishment, like Rahm Emanuel, who are dependent on billionaire campaign contributors and want to maintain the status quo. Then you have a progressive movement, which, by the way, what is getting these guys nervous is we are winning all over this country. It's not only Mamdani in New York City. It's in New Jersey. It's in Ohio. It's in Colorado. People are sick and tired of the Rahm Emanuels and the Democratic establishment and the Republican establishment. They are asking simple questions.

HILL: How do you see this playing out?

CAPUTO: I see it as a sort of a -- the Democrats catching up to where Republicans were in 2010. I mean it's been written about and said about a little is that this is sort of the Democratic Party's Tea Party movement. And, I mean, obviously their version of it.

This, to a degree, is perceived in the Trump White House as a possible advantage because they think, well, we've always accused Democrats of being communists. Now they're actually picking communists. Chevalier is the example in New York. I'm not sure how fully accurate it is, but that's going to be the battle line that the Republicans are going to be drawing with the Democrats.

FISCHER: I just want to remind people, though, in November what we were talking about was this becoming the big tent party, right? Mikie Sherrill in New Jersey, Abigail Spanberger (ph) in Virginia. This was not just about bringing in Democrats that were super far left. These are women with military track records. And so, I think that the Democrats got to figure out a way to get back to that narrative of, no, no, no, we're the big tent party, right? We can bring on a Mamdani and that works for New York City, but that's not going to work in a place like Virginia, which is a purple state.

HILL: Right. And that that's OK. I thought it was fascinating too, there was some reporting in "The New York Times" talking about the rise of Democratic socialists, specifically in the state of New York, right, and their influence. And in talking to the chair of the Democratic Party in the state, right, he, Jay Jacobs, who raised the concern, saying, look, I like some of what they're doing. But the issue here, and I'm quoting him, he said, "too often they look at moderate Democrats as the greater enemy than Republicans. They don't appeal to people in the middle. Most Americans are moderate." I mean, how much of a concern for Democrats, right, to your point about big tent, is that this is going so far to the left that they're actually looking at Democrats, moderate Democrats, as more of an enemy than Republicans?

DAVISON: That's a huge problem. I mean, if you're done with the midterms and just want to focus on 2028, just watch this debate. This is what is going to be sort of the central theme, you know, after we get through these November elections.

DAVISON: But, you know, there's a prime example in AOC, who was sort of the -- at the vanguard of this whole, you know, progressive movement, of, you know, unseating a long-standing incumbent. She is now facing questions of, is she progressive enough? Is she doing enough for the party? You know, this is, you know, a cyclical thing we see in politics all the time. But if you have someone like AOC getting questions, if her bona fides are true, if she's really committed to the DSA mission, that's a problem for the party.

HILL: And meanwhile you have the, you know, administration and likely most Republicans across the country just sitting back and popping popcorn.

CHAMBERS: I was laughing. I said if you're done with '26 and just want to talk about 2020, because you guys knew I wanted to talk about 2020 at this point.

HILL: I knew you wanted to talk to. That's going to be your next question. Don't worry.

CHAMBERS: I know -- I know and next time -- or next time.

But listen, the administration, as Marc was saying, is sitting back and saying that this is going to be their midterm message at this point, right? You've seen the president. You've seen House Speaker Mike Johnson, a number of other Republicans saying that they're Marxists, they're communists, you know, they're socialists, that they're going to, you know, you're going to be living in squalor I think is what the president said two years from now. They're saying it's free, but it won't be free. I mean that is exactly what the midterm message is right now coming from Republicans.

As far as Democrats go, though, I mean, there is this intraparty debate about the future of the -- of the Democratic Party right now and what they want it to look like. And even if Hakeem Jeffries does take over of the House, I mean he's going to have a similar problem to Mike Johnson on his hands --

CHAMBERS: Where he could only have a margin of a couple. And he's going to have to, you know, barter with them to get things done.

HILL: We're -- CHAMBERS: If he's -- if he's -- if he's the leader, because they won't even commit to making him the leader.

CAPUTO: But the future of the party might be AOC. I mean, I know you don't want to talk about 2028, but the idea that --

HILL: Francesca very much wants to talk about it, actually.

CAPUTO: Right. Well, the idea that the Democratic socialists now think she's not socialisty (ph) enough sort of puts her in the middle to a degree and that's not a bad spot for AOC to be as a 2028 cycle dawns after 2026.

HILL: So, we only have a minute left, so it's hard to get to everybody's group chat, but because we've been teasing it so much, I will say, Francesca's group chat is all about 2028.

CHAMBERS: Yes. So, Democrats set their 2028 presidential calendar on Friday evening. You may have missed it because it was a Friday night.

Three Dead, Several Injured In Shooting At Seattle Food Festival; Pentagon Updates Casualty Database to 600 Plus Wounded, 18 Killed; 300,000 Plus People Evacuated Amid Wildfires In France. Aired 6-6:30a ET

Aired July 27, 2026 - 06:00   ET

THIS IS A RUSH TRANSCRIPT. THIS COPY MAY NOT BE IN ITS FINAL FORM AND MAY BE UPDATED.

ERICA HILL, CNN ANCHOR: Breaking news overnight. A family event turning tragic after shooting leaves three people dead at a food festival in Seattle.

UNIDENTIFIED MALE: I saw families, kids, everyone just like running out of the -- out of the fair.

HILL: More than 300,000 people forced to evacuate as wildfires scorched across Europe. Why officials say the crisis there is far from over.

COL. CEDRIC LEIGHTON (RET.), CNN MILITARY ANALYST: This is where Pentagon bureaucracy meets the reality of -- of families who are grieving.

HILL: The human cost of the war in Iran increasing as the Pentagon revises the number of injured. Are Americans getting the full picture of this war?

Rahm Emanuel says progressives could cost Democrats the midterms. Bernie Sanders says, they're the party's future. So, who's right?

UNIDENTIFIED MALE: (INAUDIBLE). I see all of them. Oh, my God. I think I got it here.

HILL: Terrifying moments in downtown Seattle at an iconic food festival as it turns into a crime scene. This morning, one suspect is on the run, the other in custody.

Good morning, everyone. I'm Erica Hill in for Audie Cornish.

We do begin with an update from police. We can tell you three people are dead, four others injured, among them a two-year-old child. This after two gunmen open fire at the annual Bite of Seattle Festival.

UNIDENTIFIED MALE: I was about 20 feet or less maybe from the -- one of the people whose shot. And I couldn't really clearly see what's on, but I ran toward the gunfire and there was a, I would say at least two dozen shots.

UNIDENTIFIED MALE: I saw families, kids, everyone just like running out of the -- out of the fair. And he had told me, like, just run, just run. Active shooter. Someone was yelling active shooter. I jumped the fence quickly and I ran.

HILL: This morning, the search is on for a suspect authorities say fled the scene. One person has been arrested. Now, police believe the two suspects may have actually been targeting each other.

ASSISTANT CHIEF TYRONE DAVIS: Right now, we believe that we have no outstanding threat to the community. We do have one suspect that is being interviewed.

We believe there is one outstanding. That is part of our investigation.

UNIDENTIFIED MALE: So, this was a shootout in Bite of Seattle?

DAVIS: There were two people who we believe were shooting at each other.

HILL: Joining me now is retired NYPD officer, Jillian Snider. Jillian, it's good to have you with us.

When we look at where things stand this morning, it does not appear, based on what we know, that the festival itself was a target. We know that one suspect, we're told, is still on the loose there. Where would your focus be this morning both in terms of that suspect but also the investigation?

JILLIAN SNIDER, RETIRED NYPD OFFICER: Good morning, Erica. So, what I would do or any investigator will do is they do have one suspect in custody, and that any information that they could get from that suspect is going to be critical.

Additionally, talking to witnesses that were there. We've already seen a few segments where people that were participating in the festival have come forward. But what's really going to be important is trying to get any available surveillance in that area to try and piece this together as we saw police have already kind of confirmed that it looks like it wasn't targeted at the festival itself. It may have been two individuals targeting one another.

So, not to minimize the situation but it doesn't seem like the festival itself was the target which is always really important for establishing motive.

HILL: Yes, absolutely. And to -- and to be able to say to the community which we heard, of course, not long after that they didn't believe there was an additional threat to the community directly.

You talked about the importance of witnesses. The -- the assistant police chief actually really pleading for witnesses to come forward. I want to play a little bit of what he had to say.

DAVIS: We have witnesses. There are witnesses. They're not coming forward. We need people to be brave to reach out to us. You can do so anonymously. We know that we have people who probably have evidence or have information that they can share with us.

HILL: You hear the assistant chief there saying, asking people to be brave to come forward. Based on what we know about this shooting, do you believe that this could be an incident where people are perhaps fearful for some reason to come forward?

SNIDER: Honestly, I don't think it's that people are fearful to come forward, because again this seemed to be two individuals targeting one another.

We have two issues here. We have a fractured relationship between community members and police and that's not isolated to Seattle. That's kind of nationwide right now.

Secondary, we have a behavioral understanding that people assume the other person is going to talk to police. I don't have to do it because someone else will do it. And that's not uncommon. That's actually very, very common in situations like this where a lot of people saw something, but they just assume another person or another bystander will talk to police and that they don't have to get involved.

It's more that an individual doesn't want to get consumed into a police investigation, having to be a potential witness, having to put their name on paper, having to potentially go to court one day. So, it's -- it's that really.

But what the assistant chief was saying is -- is really important because in a situation like this, witness statements and surveillance, other than suspect information, witnesses are key and vital to ongoing investigations like this.

HILL: Yes, absolutely. And we'll be watching for any developments, of course, throughout the day, as they continue to look for that one other suspect. Jillian, appreciate it. Thank you.

SNIDER: Thank you, Erica.

HILL: Ahead here on "CNN This Morning," an update to the casualty count now for the war with Iran. Why the Pentagon's new math is raising new questions.

And a bit later, Mayor Mamdani called him a war criminal. Now, Benjamin Netanyahu is firing back.

MIKE WALTZ, UNITED STATES AMBASSADOR TO THE UNITED NATIONS:What the president is doing right now, as we've seen all along, is giving some talks, some space. Talks are ongoing. They're happening at every level.

HILL: After two straight weeks of bombing Iran, the Trump administration taking a pause, but also warning every option to hit Iran is still on the table.

Now, meantime, the full cost of this war is becoming clear. Over the weekend, the Pentagon quietly updated the total injuries and casualties since the start of Operation Epic Fury.

An online Defense Department database now lists more than 600 wounded. That's up from 482 just last week. It also lists the total number of troops killed as 18. This coming on the heels of outrage, frankly, over the Pentagon removing four names from the war's official death toll. The deaths of those service members have been reinstated but in a new category.

The Trump administration telling Congress that Operation Epic Fury is over and new operation is now underway.

LEIGHTON: These databases should really be reflecting reality, regardless of the political niceties of the War Powers Act or, you know, which operation you're in, whether it's Epic Fury or the follow on to Epic Fury or something else.

The key thing is that these databases be accurate and that they reflect the true nature of the cost of war.

Joining me now in the Group Chat, Sara Fischer, CNN senior media analyst and senior media reporter at "Axios." Laura Davison, Washington deputy bureau chief at Bloomberg News. And Francesca Chambers, White House correspondent at "USA Today."

The fact that the Defense Department is classifying deaths, injuries in a different way, also looking to do Overseas Operation versus Operation Epic Fury. That has a really significant impact, Francesca.

FRANCESCA CHAMBERS, WHITE HOUSE CORRESPONDENT, USA TODAY: And this also comes after President Trump himself said that the number was 18 last week, while he was justifying the ongoing war in Iran and -- and defending it, especially after the House had just taken that vote to say that the operations should not continue in Iran.

He said that it was 18 compared to some of these other wars that lasted years and had thousands of deaths. So, you know, just putting that out there as an acknowledgement from the president himself of what the death toll in this war has been.

Now, as far as how they're trying to reclassify it at the Pentagon, you know, I was speaking to House Speaker Mike Johnson earlier in the month and he -- or at the end of last month, you know, and he had also said that -- that -- that he thought that the 60-day clock on this would restart if the Trump administration had the ceasefire break down and then restart. That seems to be the -- the argument that the Trump administration is trying to make now, which is that this is a new conflict. Clocks restarted on this congressional approval timeframe.

HILL: It is fascinating, though, to watch the -- the back and forth here. I mean, this is right and certainly the backlash that we saw. This is all entirely of the administration are making, message-wise.

SARA FISCHER, CNN SENIOR MEDIA ANALYST: Yes. And it's part of a larger communications failure around the war. It's not just deaths. It's also how and when does this ceasefire actually start, when does it conclude.

I think that the American people are not naive. They look at this conflict in its totality, which is it didn't have to be a war of it our making. It was a war by choice, as the Democrats are saying. And they don't really care whether or not a death occurred in one part of the war or after a ceasefire.

They just want to understand holistically how many people were hurt, how many people were killed.

It also matters a lot for congressional funding. Because when you're asking Congress for money, one of the things that you have to consider, if you're a member is, do we need to give more funding to protect people's lives?

Well, if you don't have a real accurate sense of how many people's lives are being impacted, how do you make those decisions?

And so this is a crisis of confidence in terms of not just how much we are reporting, but also how we're communicating it. I don't think the American people are buying necessarily this reclassification of the numbers.

HILL: Any administration that likes to build itself is the most transparent, right, in history and you're dealing with the Pentagon that is not frankly transparent and is not as forthcoming with information and in making themselves as available.

There have also been -- there has also been reporting about some pushback from Vice President Vance, as well as General Caine. And questions about the stockpile that the U.S. military has. And Mike Waltz addressed some of that over the weekend. I just want to play what he have to say.

WALTZ: We don't have that. But -- but so -- so Mike Waltz, the U.S. ambassador to the U.N., was asked specifically about the low stockpiles. One of the things that he noted, I'm paraphrasing here was that part of the reason the stockpiles were so low was because of the Ukraine war, because of decisions made under President Biden's administration.

You know, and speaking with military officials, it's not really that -- that simple. The fact though that the stockpiles are being questioned, how does that add to complications for this administration, when there are questions about just how prepared and for how long the U.S. could be involved?

LAURA DAVISON, WASHINGTON DEPUTY BUREAU CHIEF, BLOOMBERG NEWS: This really just shows how few options the administration has at this moment. This is kind of a classic supply and demand problem of there aren't enough missiles that can be resupplied. The defense contractors have been to the White House multiple times. Trump has really been hurrying them to produce faster, but there's lots of regulations. They have to be produced domestically. They just can't keep up with the -- the speed at which they're being used.

Secondly, the Pentagon is also needing more money. You know, you've seen Hegseth up on the Hill, asking for $70 billion more to fund this war.

The administration doesn't really either have control over, you know, the production of these or the -- the -- the money, that -- that's Congress' job. All they can do is control how quickly they're using them.

So, we're seeing now, you know, that at least there -- there are reports that they're talking about rationing them to, you know, be able to, you know, have a war that was supposed to last four to six weeks. Now, we're in that four to six months range. And who really knows where this ends?

HILL: We were told to over the -- over the weekend, this is a pause, right, to allow diplomatic efforts to continue.

Is there a sense that there's any change in those diplomatic efforts? Any change in the part of the United States or even Iran on what is potentially being offered?

CHAMBERS: I mean, we've seen this repeatedly, right, that the -- the negotiations are on, the negotiations are off, then the U.S. was, you know, was bombing for nearly two straight weeks every single night, trying to force Iran to get back to the table.

So, it's -- it's very difficult to say at this point where these talks, you know, stand and how much longer we expect the war to go on.

On the munitions stockpiles, though, I just want to add, that, you know, allies around the world are -- are concerned, I think, about the munitions levels in case of another potential conflict breaking out somewhere else.

The United States is, you know, having to tap into some of the munitions that it has in other places. You've got countries like Ukraine where it isn't being given stockpiles from the U.S. anymore. It is buying those through NATO, but asking to co-produce missiles and weapons with the United States now, just saying, let us produce them at this point. We can do it just as quickly. And so this is part of a broader argument about readiness around the world for conflicts.

Still ahead here after the break on "CNN This Morning," we are going to take a closer look at those wildfires forcing mass evacuations across Europe, some of the largest evacuations since World War II, hot weather moving in to the region for this week, making those conditions for crews all the more complicated.

Also, what Trump's border czar is now admitting about the ICE officer connected to a deadly shooting in Maine.

HILL: Wildfires raging across Europe, scorching thousands of acres, forcing mass evacuations in France. Nearly 300,000 people have been displaced. It is the country's largest displacement since World War II.

Several villages reduced to ash, ghost towns, firefighters facing challenging conditions with rising temperatures, more hot weather on the forecast for those fire zones, and no rain on the horizon. France itself has already recorded more than 300 wildfires this year.

And the situation, fairly similar in Spain. Wildfires also raging there. Temperatures expected to hover around 100 degrees Fahrenheit for the next few days.

In Spain, more than 100,000 people have been evacuated. Nearly 30,000 of them from Madrid alone. Firefighters are really focused on the city, on these individual fires that are burning around Madrid, and they're trying to keep them from merging. This morning, officials say those flames are advancing more slowly, but they are still active and uncontrolled. We do know at least one person has died. That death connected now to the wildfires.

And there are more wildfires than normal this summer. If you think that's what it seems like, you're right. All of this really related to climate change. We had an abnormally wet winter, record hot summer, really dry fueling these flames.

CNN international correspondent Pau Mosquera joining us now from just outside Madrid.

This is such a battle for firefighters. Where do things stand right now on the ground, Pau?

PAU MOSQUERA, CNN INTERNATIONAL CORRESPONDENT: Well, we know, Erica, that overnight, firefighters have been working nonstop to try to control the different fires that are now devastating the region of Madrid.

Actually, we are in Navas del Rey. This is the closest that could -- we could get to one of the active fire fronts that are now burning in the region. And you can see the presence of the fire because of the tower of smoke that is behind me.

Have a look here. Twenty kilometers far from the area where right now the fire is burning. You can see the presence of this thick column of smoke that is marking the place where right now all the devastation is happening.

And I can tell you, Erica, that we are constantly hearing and seeing planes and helicopters flying overhead as they are going to San Juan Reservoir, which is just a few meters from where we are to get some water and drop on the top of the flames in that area that we are showing here.

But it's important to say, Erica, that this place, Navas del Rey, was already affected for the blaze a few days ago. You can see actually the aftermath of the flames here. The ground looks completely black.

And actually some houses in the area, in the region, were completely damaged because the advance of the flames.

Right now, the authority say today, Monday, it's going to be quite a complicated day because they are expecting wind gusts of up to 30 kilometers per hour, which should and may complicate things a little bit.

And as you were saying, also, we're expecting from Wednesday and on another heat wave here in Spain. So, the temperatures, again, are going to climb, Erica.

HILL: Absolutely. Not ideal conditions to put it mildly. Pau, appreciate it. Thank you. Straight ahead here on "CNN This Morning," we'll take a closer look at the extreme weather here at home. Millions of Americans baking under yet another dangerous heat dome.

Plus, after weeks of war with Iran, concerns are mounting as we were discussing over the weapon supply.

Vance and Caine Raised Concerns about Escalating the War; Netanyahu Heads to the U.S.; ICE Vetting Under Review; Sanders Defends Progressive Candidates. Aired 6:30-7a ET

Aired July 27, 2026 - 06:30   ET

THIS IS A RUSH TRANSCRIPT. THIS COPY MAY NOT BE IN ITS FINAL FORM AND MAY BE UPDATED.

ERICA HILL, CNN ANCHOR: Good morning. Half past the hour here on your Monday. I'm Erica Hill, in for Audie Cornish. Thanks for joining us on CNN THIS MORNING.

The breaking news this morning, the search for a second suspect involved in the deadly mass shooting at a food festival in Seattle underway. One suspect is in custody. Police say three people were killed, multiple others injured, including a two-year-old child, when gunfire broke out. Police believe they may have been innocent bystanders and that the shooters were likely not targeting the festival but targeting each other.

Opening statements set to begin this morning in the trial of the Massachusetts mother who's accused of killing her three young children. This happened in 2023. Prosecutors say Lindsay Clancy planned the killings of her children, but the defense argues she was suffering from severe postpartum psychosis.

It is another day of extreme heat for much of the central and southern parts of the country. You can see that on the map there. Millions under heat warnings. Officials say a heat dome with a heat index of up to 118 degrees in some places. Those temperatures are expected to dip by the middle of the week, but they could climb back up by the weekend.

The temporary pause in U.S. strikes on Iran does seem to be holding at this hour amid growing concerns over the conflict escalating further. vocabulary.en: to limit the amount of something that someone is allowed to have

vocabulary.en: relating to the management of relations between countries

vocabulary.en: to force people to leave their homes
vocabulary.excerpt: Nearly 300,000 people have been displaced.

vocabulary.en: a town that has been abandoned by its inhabitants

vocabulary.excerpt: Millions of Americans baking under yet another dangerous heat dome.

vocabulary.en: to move forward

vocabulary.en: the situation that exists after a bad event
vocabulary.excerpt: the aftermath of the flames

vocabulary.excerpt: carrying out more aggressive moves could further deplete stockpiles
vocabulary.example_cn: 执行更激进的行动可能会进一步耗尽库存。

vocabulary.en: a missile or aircraft used to intercept and destroy enemy weapons
vocabulary.excerpt: it's not just U.S. forces that use these expensive interceptors

vocabulary.en: the act of spending or using money, time, or resources
vocabulary.excerpt: it requires the expenditure of these scarce resources
vocabulary.example_cn: 这需要消耗这些稀缺资源。

vocabulary.en: a situation in which there is less of something than is needed
vocabulary.excerpt: the shortfalls in the defense industrial base have been long standing
vocabulary.example_cn: 国防工业基础的短缺问题由来已久。

vocabulary.en: to reduce the quality, value, or effectiveness of something
vocabulary.excerpt: we've degraded that considerably
vocabulary.example_cn: 我们已经大大削弱了它。

vocabulary.en: a long-term goal that is part of a plan
vocabulary.excerpt: We haven't achieved our strategic aims.
vocabulary.example_cn: 我们尚未实现战略目标。

vocabulary.cn: 存在主义的，关乎生存的
vocabulary.en: relating to existence, especially human existence
vocabulary.excerpt: this is an existential fight for the survival of the state
vocabulary.example_cn: 这是一场关乎国家存亡的斗争。

vocabulary.en: a method of calculation or reasoning
vocabulary.excerpt: your calculus is different
vocabulary.example_cn: 你的考量是不同的。

vocabulary.en: a time of significant change in a situation
vocabulary.excerpt: Is this an inflection point for the mayor
vocabulary.example_cn: 这对市长来说是一个转折点吗？

vocabulary.en: the process of examining someone or something carefully to decide if they are suitable
vocabulary.excerpt: Did the vetting process fail?
vocabulary.example_cn: 审查过程失败了吗？

vocabulary.en: to give up something, such as a possession or a right
vocabulary.excerpt: A judge later ordered he relinquished any firearms.
vocabulary.example_cn: 法官后来命令他交出所有枪支。

vocabulary.en: an event that happens only once and is not part of a pattern
vocabulary.excerpt: Is it an isolated instance or could there be a bigger problem brewing?
vocabulary.example_cn: 这是一个孤立事件，还是可能有更大的问题在酝酿？

vocabulary.en: a fixed amount or number that is officially allowed
vocabulary.excerpt: they wanted to make up that quota that President Trump has set
vocabulary.example_cn: 他们想达到特朗普总统设定的配额。

vocabulary.en: a noticeable difference or disagreement between people or groups
vocabulary.excerpt: We're starting to see some daylight between ICE and Homan and the White House
vocabulary.example_cn: 我们开始看到ICE、霍曼和白宫之间出现一些分歧。

vocabulary.cn: 绝对可靠的，不会犯错的
vocabulary.en: never making mistakes or being wrong
vocabulary.excerpt: ICE has, in his mind, sort of been infallible here
vocabulary.example_cn: 在他看来，ICE在这里几乎是不会犯错的。

vocabulary.cn: 过于冒进，超出能力范围
vocabulary.en: to do something too quickly or without enough preparation
vocabulary.excerpt: we may have gotten over our skis a little bit
vocabulary.example_cn: 我们可能有点过于冒进了。

vocabulary.en: evidence that someone is who they say they are or that something is true
vocabulary.excerpt: if her bona fides are true
vocabulary.example_cn: 如果她的诚意是真的。

vocabulary.en: the leading position in a movement or field
vocabulary.excerpt: AOC, who was sort of the at the vanguard of this whole progressive movement
vocabulary.example_cn: AOC，她可以说是整个进步运动的先锋。

vocabulary.en: to remove someone from a position of power
vocabulary.excerpt: unseating a long-standing incumbent
vocabulary.example_cn: 罢免一位长期任职的在位者。

vocabulary.en: occurring within a political party
vocabulary.excerpt: there is this intraparty debate about the future of the Democratic Party
vocabulary.example_cn: 党内关于民主党未来的辩论正在进行。

vocabulary.en: to exchange goods or services for other goods or services without using money
vocabulary.excerpt: he's going to have to barter with them to get things done
vocabulary.example_cn: 他将不得不与他们讨价还价才能完成事情。

vocabulary.en: a list of things to be discussed or dealt with
vocabulary.excerpt: On the docket, he has a meeting with President Trump
vocabulary.example_cn: 议程上，他与特朗普总统有一次会面。

vocabulary.en: a person who advocates aggressive or warlike policies
vocabulary.excerpt: Lindsey Graham as a hawk
vocabulary.example_cn: 林赛·格雷厄姆作为鹰派人物。

vocabulary.cn: 制度主义者，重视机构的人
vocabulary.en: a person who believes in the importance of established institutions
vocabulary.excerpt: he was both an institutionalist
vocabulary.example_cn: 他既是一个制度主义者。

vocabulary.en: a point on which something turns or depends
vocabulary.excerpt: this really presents a potential pivot point for U.S. foreign policy
vocabulary.example_cn: 这确实为美国外交政策提供了一个潜在的转折点。

vocabulary.en: a long list of things that need to be done or considered
vocabulary.excerpt: there's a whole laundry list of things
vocabulary.example_cn: 有一长串的事情。

vocabulary.en: to take someone away from a group to speak to them privately
vocabulary.excerpt: is this going to be a pull aside at the funeral
vocabulary.example_cn: 这是在葬礼上私下交谈吗？

vocabulary.en: a short, unimportant argument
vocabulary.excerpt: Across the summer we've seen various spats
vocabulary.example_cn: 整个夏天我们看到了各种小争吵。

vocabulary.en: the general shape or outline of something
vocabulary.excerpt: The contours of what that end state looks like may differ for us
vocabulary.example_cn: 最终状态的轮廓对我们来说可能不同。

sentences.en: This is where Pentagon bureaucracy meets the reality of families who are grieving.
sentences.cn: 这就是五角大楼的官僚机构与悲痛家庭现实相遇的地方。
sentences.structure: 主系表结构，where引导表语从句，who引导定语从句修饰families
sentences.analysis: 句子主干为This is where...，where引导的表语从句说明地点或情况，who引导的定语从句修饰families，说明这些家庭正在悲痛。

sentences.en: The Trump administration telling Congress that Operation Epic Fury is over and new operation is now underway.
sentences.cn: 特朗普政府告诉国会，‘史诗之怒’行动已经结束，新的行动正在进行中。
sentences.structure: 主谓宾结构，现在分词短语作谓语，that引导宾语从句
sentences.analysis: 主语The Trump administration，谓语telling，间接宾语Congress，直接宾语为that引导的从句，从句中and连接两个并列句。

sentences.en: These databases should really be reflecting reality, regardless of the political niceties of the War Powers Act or, you know, which operation you're in, whether it's Epic Fury or the follow on to Epic Fury or something else.
sentences.cn: 这些数据库应该真实反映现实，无论《战争权力法》的政治细节如何，或者，你知道，无论你处于哪个行动中，无论是‘史诗之怒’还是其后续行动或其他什么。
sentences.structure: 主谓宾结构，regardless of引导让步状语，whether...or...引导选择状语
sentences.analysis: 主干为These databases should be reflecting reality，regardless of...为让步状语，其中包含which引导的宾语从句和whether...or...结构。

sentences.en: The fact that the Defense Department is classifying deaths, injuries in a different way, also looking to do Overseas Operation versus Operation Epic Fury, that has a really significant impact, Francesca.
sentences.cn: 国防部以不同方式分类死亡和受伤，还试图区分‘海外行动’和‘史诗之怒’行动，这一事实具有重大影响，弗朗西斯卡。
sentences.structure: 同位语从句，主语为The fact，that引导同位语从句，主句为that has a really significant impact
sentences.analysis: The fact后接that引导的同位语从句，说明事实内容，主句为that has...，其中that指代前文事实。

sentences.en: He said that it was 18 compared to some of these other wars that lasted years and had thousands of deaths.
sentences.cn: 他说，与那些持续数年、造成数千人死亡的其他战争相比，这个数字是18。
sentences.structure: 主谓宾结构，that引导宾语从句，compared to...作状语，that引导定语从句修饰wars
sentences.analysis: 主干He said that...，宾语从句中compared to...为比较状语，that lasted...为定语从句修饰wars。

sentences.en: Now, as far as how they're trying to reclassify it at the Pentagon, you know, I was speaking to House Speaker Mike Johnson earlier in the month and he had also said that he thought that the 60-day clock on this would restart if the Trump administration had the ceasefire break down and then restart.
sentences.cn: 现在，至于五角大楼如何试图重新分类，你知道，我本月早些时候与众议院议长迈克·约翰逊交谈过，他也说过，他认为如果特朗普政府的停火破裂然后重新开始，这个60天时钟将重新启动。
sentences.structure: 复合句，as far as引导状语从句，主句为I was speaking...，and连接并列句，that引导宾语从句，if引导条件状语从句
sentences.analysis: as far as...引导状语从句，主句为I was speaking...，and后he had said that...，that从句中包含that引导的宾语从句和if引导的条件状语从句。

sentences.en: It also matters a lot for congressional funding because when you're asking Congress for money, one of the things that you have to consider, if you're a member is, do we need to give more funding to protect people's lives?
sentences.cn: 这对国会拨款也很重要，因为当你向国会要钱时，如果你是议员，你必须考虑的一件事是，我们是否需要提供更多资金来保护人们的生命？
sentences.structure: 主谓宾结构，because引导原因状语从句，when引导时间状语从句，that引导定语从句，if引导条件状语从句
sentences.analysis: 主干It matters...，because引导原因状语从句，从句中when引导时间状语，that引导定语从句修饰things，if引导条件状语。

sentences.en: The administration doesn't really either have control over, you know, the production of these or the money, that's Congress' job.
sentences.cn: 政府实际上既无法控制这些武器的生产，也无法控制资金，那是国会的工作。
sentences.structure: 主谓宾结构，either...or...连接并列宾语，that's Congress' job为补充说明
sentences.analysis: 主语The administration，谓语doesn't have control over，宾语为either...or...连接的两个名词短语，后面that's...为独立分句。

sentences.en: We were told to over the weekend, this is a pause, right, to allow diplomatic efforts to continue.
sentences.cn: 我们在周末被告知，这是一个暂停，对吧，以允许外交努力继续。
sentences.structure: 被动语态，主谓宾结构，不定式短语作目的状语
sentences.analysis: 主干We were told，to over the weekend为时间状语，this is a pause为直接引语，to allow...为目的状语。

sentences.en: The United States is having to tap into some of the munitions that it has in other places.
sentences.cn: 美国不得不动用其在其他地方的一些弹药。
sentences.structure: 主谓宾结构，that引导定语从句修饰munitions
sentences.analysis: 主干The United States is having to tap into...，that引导定语从句修饰munitions，说明弹药所在位置。

sentences.en: Sources telling CNN, the president was briefed by Vice President J.D. Vance and Joint Chiefs Chairman Dan Caine on Friday.
sentences.cn: 消息人士告诉CNN，总统周五听取了副总统J.D.万斯和参谋长联席会议主席丹·凯恩的简报。
sentences.structure: 主谓宾+宾语补足语（telling CNN + 宾语从句）
sentences.analysis: 现在分词短语'Sources telling CNN'作独立主格结构，主句为'the president was briefed...'，被动语态。

sentences.en: The general reportedly telling Trump that carrying out more aggressive moves could further deplete stockpiles, along with other potential downsides.
sentences.cn: 据报道，这位将军告诉特朗普，执行更激进的行动可能会进一步耗尽库存，并带来其他潜在负面影响。
sentences.structure: 主谓宾+宾语从句（telling Trump that...）
sentences.analysis: 现在分词短语'telling Trump that...'作伴随状语，宾语从句中主语为动名词短语'carrying out more aggressive moves'。

sentences.en: And it's important to remember that it's not just U.S. forces that use these expensive interceptors, but also our gulf partners.
sentences.cn: 重要的是要记住，使用这些昂贵拦截器的不仅仅是美军，还有我们的海湾伙伴。
sentences.structure: It is + adj. + to do + that从句（强调结构）
sentences.analysis: 形式主语it，真正主语为不定式短语'to remember...'，that从句中使用'not just...but also...'结构。

sentences.en: And each time that Iran launches missiles or one way attack drones, it requires the expenditure of these scarce resources.
sentences.cn: 每次伊朗发射导弹或单向攻击无人机，都需要消耗这些稀缺资源。
sentences.structure: 时间状语从句+主句
sentences.analysis: each time引导时间状语从句，主句主语it指代前文提到的行动。

sentences.en: But, two, certainly I think the initial planning for this campaign did not anticipate that it would go this long.
sentences.cn: 但第二点，我认为这次行动的初步规划没有预料到会持续这么久。
sentences.structure: 主谓宾+宾语从句（think + that从句）
sentences.analysis: 主句'I think'后接省略that的宾语从句，从句中'anticipate'后接that宾语从句。

sentences.en: And when I, as an intelligence professional, look at an enemy's -- what they might do, I look at two things.
sentences.cn: 当我作为一名情报专业人士审视敌人——他们可能做什么时，我会看两件事。
sentences.structure: 时间状语从句+主句
sentences.analysis: when引导时间状语从句，插入语'as an intelligence professional'，主句为'I look at two things'。

sentences.en: And in terms of their ability to do so, we've degraded that considerably, but not eliminated it.
sentences.cn: 就他们这样做的能力而言，我们已经大大削弱了它，但并未消除它。
sentences.structure: 介词短语+并列句
sentences.analysis: 介词短语'in terms of...'作状语，并列句由but连接，前后形成对比。

sentences.en: They are not making the kind of calculations that a nation who put their economic likelihood as their top priority would make.
sentences.cn: 他们并没有做出那种将经济可能性作为首要任务的国家会做出的计算。
sentences.structure: 主谓宾+定语从句
sentences.analysis: 主句主语They，谓语are not making，宾语calculations后接that引导的定语从句，从句中嵌套who引导的定语从句修饰a nation。

sentences.en: But when you're in an existential fight for the survival of the Islamic Republic, your calculus is different.
sentences.cn: 但当你处于为伊斯兰共和国生存而战的斗争中时，你的考量是不同的。
sentences.structure: 时间状语从句+主句
sentences.analysis: when引导时间状语从句，主句为'your calculus is different'。

sentences.en: And there are very few senators left in that role.
sentences.cn: 而剩下能扮演这个角色的参议员寥寥无几。
sentences.structure: There be句型+过去分词短语作定语
sentences.analysis: There be句型，主语senators后接过去分词短语'left in that role'作定语。

sentences.en: You know, there's a whole laundry list of things that the president has talked about that, you know, may shift, you know, depending at least on Capitol Hill where his party is.
sentences.cn: 你知道，总统谈到过一长串事情，这些事情可能会发生变化，至少取决于国会山他所在政党的立场。
sentences.structure: There be句型+定语从句+状语从句
sentences.analysis: There be句型，主语list后接that引导的定语从句，从句中嵌套where引导的定语从句修饰Capitol Hill。

sentences.en: But it certainly is an opportunity for President Trump and Bibi Netanyahu to get back on the same page again, right?
sentences.cn: 但这无疑是特朗普总统和比比·内塔尼亚胡再次达成一致的机会，对吧？
sentences.structure: 主系表+不定式短语作定语
sentences.analysis: 主句主语it，系动词is，表语opportunity，后接不定式短语'for...to get back...'作定语。

sentences.en: And so there may be a concern, as Iran's strategy all along has been to make this so politically and economically untenable for us that we back off on some of the concessions we're demanding.
sentences.cn: 因此，可能存在一种担忧，即伊朗的策略一直是让这件事在政治和经济上对我们来说如此难以为继，以至于我们放弃一些我们要求的让步。
sentences.structure: 主句+as引导的原因状语从句+so...that...结构
sentences.analysis: 主句'there may be a concern'，as引导原因状语从句，从句中使用'so...that...'结构，that从句中嵌套定语从句'we're demanding'修饰concessions。

sentences.en: There could be concerns on the part of Israel and gulf states that we come to an agreement with Iran that leaves dangerous capabilities that continue to threaten them.
sentences.cn: 以色列和海湾国家可能担心我们与伊朗达成一项协议，该协议留下继续威胁他们的危险能力。
sentences.structure: There be句型+同位语从句+定语从句
sentences.analysis: There be句型，主语concerns后接that引导的同位语从句，从句中嵌套that引导的定语从句修饰agreement，再嵌套that引导的定语从句修饰capabilities。

sentences.en: And I think that the Democrats got to figure out a way to get back to that narrative of, no, no, no, we're the big tent party, right?
sentences.cn: 我认为民主党必须想办法回到那种叙事：不，不，不，我们是包容性的大党，对吧？
sentences.structure: 主谓宾+宾语从句
sentences.analysis: 主句'I think'后接that宾语从句，从句中不定式短语'to figure out a way'作宾语，后接不定式短语'to get back...'作定语。

topics.title: US-Iran War and Weapon Stockpile
topics.content: 美国对伊朗的军事行动持续，特朗普政府称‘史诗之怒’行动结束，新行动开始。美军武器库存紧张，国防承包商加速生产，但供应仍不足。国会要求更多资金。
